passage:
Age two: Jagdish points at the moon from his father's shoulders and cries, "Aai, chanda, see, moon!" Marathi from his grandmother, Hindi from the neighbours, English from the picture book, all in one breath. His parents grin and say, "Yes, chanda, the moon," and leave it there.

Age fifteen: Jomon's group chat runs on "Yaar, that quiz was too tough, bilkul nahi aaya" and "chill kar, party toh banti hai." Nobody thinks about it; it sounds like being part of the same crowd. When his class announces mock interviews, he practises alone in front of the mirror, dropping the slang and speaking in plain, tidy English.

Age twenty: Ganga wears a Malayalam poetry T-shirt in her Delhi hostel and bristles when a notice goes up only in Hindi. She argues about it loudly at dinner, proud and a little fierce. Later she teaches her roommate Asha, from Lucknow, how to say "nandi", and learns "chalo, khana thanda ho raha hai" in return. They laugh at each other's accents until the mess hall closes.

qa.q: What did two-year-old Jagdish say while pointing at the moon?
qa.a: Jagdish said, "Aai, chanda, see, moon!", using Marathi, Hindi and English words in one breath.

qa.q: How do Jagdish at two, Jomon at fifteen and Ganga at twenty each relate to language differently?
qa.a: Jagdish mixes Marathi, Hindi and English while sorting sounds; Jomon's slang belongs with friends, but he practises plain English for interviews; Ganga is proud of Malayalam and still trades words with Asha.

qa.q: What is Ganga feeling when the notice appears only in Hindi?
qa.a: Ganga feels irritated and fiercely proud of Malayalam, as if her language is being pushed aside, yet she stays warm toward Asha.

qa.q: Why does Jomon practise in tidy English before the mock interviews?
qa.a: Slang works with friends, but interviews ask for a cleaner way of speaking, so practising it lets Jomon use both styles when they fit.

grounding: A progression of one language theme from a toddler mixing tongues, to a teen's playful Hinglish with a register switch, to a young adult's regional pride that still crosses language lines.

passage:
Baby Pema was fourteen months old when her grandfather Bhupen leaned over her cot each morning. Her whole face opened: mouth wide, eyes crinkled, both fists waving. Bhupen smiled back just as widely and said, "There you are!" She squealed, and the two of them went on trading looks until the kettle whistled.

Seven years later Pema stood at the door of a new school, holding her bag strap with both hands. The teacher, Siddharth, said, "Good morning, Pema, welcome." Her lips pressed together into a small, neat smile, and her eyes dropped to her shoes.

Siddharth did not say, "Come on, give me a big smile." He nodded, pointed at a desk by the window and said, "That one is yours whenever you are ready to sit." Pema let out a breath, walked over and unzipped her bag. By lunch she had shown a classmate her pencil case, and her smile had grown, though only by a little.

qa.q: Who leaned over Pema's cot each morning when she was fourteen months old?
qa.a: Her grandfather Bhupen leaned over her cot each morning.

qa.q: How does Pema's smile at fourteen months differ from her smile at seven years, and what changed in how the adult answered?
qa.a: As a baby she gave a wide, open smile that Bhupen matched, building a back-and-forth of attention; at school she gave a small closed smile of shyness, and Siddharth gave her time instead of asking for more.

qa.q: What was Pema likely feeling as she stood at the new classroom door?
qa.a: Pema was probably shy and unsure, gripping her bag strap and looking at her shoes, yet polite enough to smile a little.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do that helped Pema settle in?
qa.a: Siddharth greeted her warmly, did not push her for a bigger smile, and pointed out her desk so she could sit when ready.

grounding: Smile variations across ages: an infant's open social smile met with warmth, and a school-age child's small closed-mouth smile of shyness met with patience.

passage:
Varun was five when the tablet went dark at dinner time. He threw himself on the hall floor, kicking the skirting board and screaming until his face went red. His mother, Leela, did not shout back. She sat on the floor a few steps away, breathed slowly and said nothing. When his sobs slowed, she brought water. Only that evening, in the lamplight, she said, "You were so angry when the show ended."

At nine, Varun heard his father, Yogesh, shouting about a cracked window. Varun's stomach dropped. He stood still, eyes fixed on the tiles, then blurted, "It wasn't me, it was the ball!" His father's voice got louder, and Varun's words tangled and stopped.

An hour later Yogesh knocked on his door, quiet now. "I was scared it might hurt someone," he said. "Tell me what happened." This time Varun listened to every word, and told him about the ball.

qa.q: What did Leela do while five-year-old Varun screamed in the hall?
qa.a: Leela sat on the floor a few steps away, breathed slowly and said nothing until his sobs slowed.

qa.q: Why could Varun take in his father's words later but not while Yogesh was shouting?
qa.a: At five Varun is kicking and screaming, and Leela sits nearby without shouting back; at nine, while his father is shouting, Varun freezes and his words tangle. In both, the talk that works comes later, when things are quiet and Varun can listen.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when his father shouted about the window?
qa.a: Varun felt frightened, his stomach dropping, and he defended himself in a rush because the loud voice left him unable to think.

qa.q: What could a parent do after a child has calmed down from a meltdown?
qa.a: A parent could name the feeling gently, as Leela did that evening, so the child learns the words for it once the storm has passed.

grounding: One child across ages meets anger twice, and in both a calm adult and a later quiet talk make understanding possible.

passage:
Age five: Jaya tells her class that a blue dragon flew through the window and ate her sandwich, then a second dragon brought it back. The teacher smiles and asks, "That is a wonderful story. Who took the sandwich in real life?" Jaya thinks and says, "Nobody, I forgot it at home."

Age fifteen: Pooja stands outside the staff room, unsure. Some older students have been climbing onto the unlocked roof, and she is also still angry at one of them about a quarrel. The teacher listens without a frown, says, "Thank you for telling me," and walks up to check the roof door that same afternoon. Pooja is not asked why she came.

Age twenty-four: On a long train ride Aparna is bubbling with a story about her messy flat share. A stranger nods along. She pauses, remembers the group photo of her housemates she nearly posted publicly, and keeps the details of the argument to herself. She tells the full story that night to her sister instead.

qa.q: What did Jaya say the blue dragon did?
qa.a: Jaya said a blue dragon flew through the window and ate her sandwich, and a second dragon brought it back.

qa.q: How does the way each person shares information differ across the three ages?
qa.a: Five-year-old Jaya blends fantasy with fact and is gently guided to separate them; fifteen-year-old Pooja reports a risk to an adult who acts without doubting her motives; twenty-four-year-old Aparna chooses how much to tell a stranger and who deserves the full story.

qa.q: What might Pooja be feeling as she waits outside the staff room?
qa.a: Pooja is probably torn, worried about the danger on the roof while still angry about the quarrel, and unsure how the telling will be seen.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that made Pooja's report useful?
qa.a: The teacher thanked Pooja, listened without guessing her motives, and checked the roof door the same afternoon.

grounding: Sharing information at three ages: a child's imaginative narration, a teenager's report to an adult, and a young adult deciding how much of a personal story to share.

passage:
Two-year-old Alka holds up her knee to her father, Bhupen. "Ouch. Slide. Scared," she says. He kneels, looks at the scrape and says, "The slide was fast, wasn't it? Let's clean it." She leans against him and leaves it there, calm again.

At fifteen, Alka stands in the kitchen doorway, twisting her sleeve. "I copied a friend's homework because I could not finish, and I feel awful." Bhupen puts down his tea. He does not raise his voice. "Tell me all of it," he says. Only after she finishes does he ask what she would like to do about it.

At twenty-four, Alka sits across from her manager, Dolma. "I made a mistake in the client sheet, and I don't yet know the newer tool well," she says. "I have fixed the figures and booked a training slot on Thursday." Dolma nods. "Thank you for telling me early. Let's pair you with someone for the first week.

qa.q: What did two-year-old Alka say when she showed her knee?
qa.a: Alka said, "Ouch. Slide. Scared." while holding up her knee to Bhupen.

qa.q: What ties Alka's confiding at two, fifteen and twenty-four together?
qa.a: Each time Alka speaks up to a listener who stays calm, first Bhupen about the scrape and about the homework, then Dolma about the sheet, which makes it easier to tell the truth again; at twenty-four she also brings a plan.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling in the kitchen doorway at fifteen?
qa.a: Alka felt guilty and anxious, twisting her sleeve as she admitted she had copied and felt awful.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's reply suit Alka's way of raising the mistake?
qa.a: Alka came early with the figures fixed and a training slot booked, and Dolma thanked her and offered support, so admitting the gap built trust rather than fear.

grounding: Self-disclosure at three ages, each met with calm listening: a toddler's brief report, a teenager's confession, and a young professional admitting a gap with a plan.

passage:
At two, Naveen rubs his eyes hard and tugs his ear while his father, Jatin, hurries through the market. Jatin checks the clock, sees it is past nap time, feels his son's forehead and finds it cool. He also notices the noisy stall next to them. "Let's find somewhere quiet," he says, and Naveen presses his face into his shoulder.

At nine, Naveen stands beside the blackboard to answer a question, twirling a lock of hair and straightening his uniform collar again and again. The teacher waits without comment and lets him finish. A classmate whispers that Naveen must not know the answer, but the answer he gives is right.

At twenty-five, at the end of a long meeting, Naveen presses his temples and rolls his neck. His colleague Wasim slides a glass of water toward him and asks quietly, "Do you want a short break, or is something else going on?" Naveen laughs tiredly. "Just the screen and the back-to-back calls," he says.

qa.q: What did Jatin check when Naveen rubbed his eyes at two?
qa.a: Jatin checked the clock and found it was past nap time, felt Naveen's forehead, and noticed the noisy stall.

qa.q: What is common to Naveen's habits at two, nine and twenty-five, and how does each adult handle them?
qa.a: At each age Naveen uses a small body movement, rubbing eyes, twirling hair, pressing temples, that could mean several things; Jatin checks the whole picture, the teacher waits, and Wasim asks kindly instead of guessing.

qa.q: What might Naveen be feeling as he stands at the blackboard at nine?
qa.a: Naveen is probably nervous and self-conscious, using the hair twirl and collar straightening to comfort himself even though he knows the answer.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that suited the situation?
qa.a: Wasim offered water and asked whether Naveen wanted a break or something else was wrong, rather than assuming the cause of the temple rubbing.

grounding: Self-directed movements across ages: a sleepy toddler's eye rubbing, a schoolchild's self-comfort with hair and uniform, and a young professional's tired temples, each read by adults who check before guessing.
